key_insight: Current T2I evaluation practices favor visually vivid, oversaturated images, causing models to produce outputs that look 'too vivid to be real.' The paper introduces a benchmark and calibration strategy to measure and correct generative color fidelity so outputs better match real-world photographic color.
problem_solved: Addresses the mismatch between human-/preference-trained evaluation and true photographic color fidelity, which leads to overly saturated/contrasty generations even when realism is intended.
method: Build a color-fidelity benchmark pairing real photographs with T2I generations and human ground-truth labels to quantify realistic color reproduction.
Develop objective color-fidelity metrics (e.g., perceptual color differences, distributional color alignment) to expose evaluation bias toward vividness.
Introduce calibration techniques (post-hoc color correction, loss re-weighting or score calibration) to align model outputs and preference metrics with real-world color statistics.
impact: Enables practitioners to reliably evaluate and adjust T2I models for realistic color reproduction, improving trustworthiness in applications that require accurate colors (e.g., product imagery, photography augmentation). It reduces reliance on misleading preference scores that reward unrealistic vividness.
visual_elements: Before/after image pairs: original model output (oversaturated) vs calibrated output (photographically faithful)
Histogram or scatter plot of color-shift metrics (e.g., ΔE) comparing models, humans, and calibrated outputs
Calibration pipeline diagram showing benchmark -> metric evaluation -> calibration step (post-processing or training)
Small icons indicating application domains (e-commerce, photography, film) to show practical relevance
paper_title: Too Vivid to Be Real? Benchmarking and Calibrating Generative Color Fidelity
paper_authors: Zhengyao Fang, Zexi Jia, Yijia Zhong, Pengcheng Luo, Jinchao Zhang
